pages.name: Two poles
pages.text: A 220 V insulated DC board has a balanced bridge. Two equal 100 kΩ arms join its poles to the hull. Each pole reads 110 V to the hull, half the bus. A lamp detector's two lamps would both glow at half brightness.

pages.alt: A 220 V insulated DC board. Two equal 100 kΩ detector arms join its positive and negative poles to the hull. The positive has no leak, and the negative has no leak. A voltmeter, ideal, joins the positive to the hull. Each pole sits half the bus from the hull. The bridge alarm is dark. The positive's lamp is 50% bright, and the negative's is 50% bright. The insulation monitor is switched off.

pages.name: A 24 V board
pages.task: A ship's automation runs on 24 V DC. Take a 24 V control board with the same kind of detector, two equal arms. Its insulation is healthy. What does each pole read to the hull?
pages.why: Equal arms split the bus evenly. Each pole sits 12 V from the hull. The two pole-to-hull voltages always add up to the bus voltage.
options: 12 V each
24 V each
0 V, as nothing is tied to the hull

pages.name: A leak on the negative
pages.text: With the negative's insulation down to 20 kΩ, its side is 16.7 kΩ. The negative reads 31.4 V to the hull and the positive reads 188.6 V.

pages.name: Which pole leaks?
pages.task: On a 220 V board, the meter reads 189 V on the positive and 31 V on the negative. Which pole has the leak?
pages.answer: The negative, as it reads low
pages.why: The pole with less resistance to the hull takes less of the voltage. The leak drags the negative towards the hull, so the positive climbs. It works like the shifting triangle, with two poles instead of three phases.

pages.name: Without a detector
pages.task: A 100 V board has no detector. Its positive leaks 500 kΩ to the hull, and its negative has fallen to 51 kΩ. What does the negative read?
pages.why: With no detector, the two leaks alone make the divider. The negative takes 100 × 51 ÷ (500 + 51) = 9.26 V.[^4] The positive reads the other 90.7 V.

pages.name: After a wash-down
pages.task: Both poles of a 220 V board read 110 V after a wash-down. Which instrument would show whether the insulation has fallen?
pages.why: The bridge and the voltmeter both compare the poles. An equal fall on both leaves the halves equal. The monitor pushes its own voltage to the hull and reads the total resistance. So it sees the fall.

pages.name: Two readings of 31.4 V
pages.task: A 220 V board has 100 kΩ arms. An old meter reads 31.4 V on the negative, then 31.4 V on the positive. What is going on?
pages.answer: The meter itself is a low path to the hull
pages.why: When two readings do not add to the bus voltage, suspect the meter. A 20 kΩ meter turns a 100 kΩ arm into 16.7 kΩ. That side takes 31.4 V. Use a high-resistance meter, and check that the pair adds up.

pages.alt: A 220 V insulated DC board. Two equal 100 kΩ detector arms join its positive and negative poles to the hull. The positive has no leak, and the negative has no leak. A voltmeter, 20 kΩ, joins the negative to the hull. The positive sits further from the hull than the negative. The bridge alarm is lit. The positive's lamp is 86% bright, and the negative's is 14% bright. The insulation monitor is switched off.
options: Both poles have leaked to 20 kΩ
The meter itself is a low path to the hull
The bus has fallen to 62.9 V

pages.name: Two detectors
pages.task: Two panels are joined into one 220 V system. Each has its own 100 kΩ detector. The negative leaks 20 kΩ to the hull. What does the negative read?
pages.why: Each side now has two 100 kΩ arms in parallel, 50 kΩ. The negative's side is 50 kΩ and 20 kΩ in parallel, 14.3 kΩ. It reads 220 × 14.3 ÷ 64.3 = 48.9 V. Every extra detector makes the same leak look smaller.

pages.name: Current into the fault
pages.task: On an insulated AC system, a first fault passes a steady current through the cables' capacitance. Now a 220 V DC board's negative has a solid fault to the hull. What flows into the fault?
pages.answer: A brief charging current, then only what the positive's paths let through
pages.why: The capacitance takes a brief charge when the fault strikes. Once charged, that path carries almost no current.[^6] After that, current runs from the positive through its 100 kΩ arm, then through the hull into the fault. That is 220 ÷ 100,000 = 2.2 mA.
